title: Curved arrows
goal: Draw curved arrows from electrons to where they go, keep every octet, and count formal charges.

problemSets.title: Sources and sinks
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: An arrow starts at electrons (a lone pair or a bond) and ends where they go.
problemSets.conceptCard:
A curved arrow shows **two electrons** moving.

- It **starts** at the electrons: a **lone pair** or a **bond**. Never at a positive charge or a bare hydrogen.
- It **ends** where the electrons go: between two atoms for a **new bond**, or on an atom for a **new lone pair**.

The **source** is electron-rich (an anion, a lone pair, a π bond). The **sink** is electron-poor (a cation, an empty orbital, an acidic H).

setItems.whyThisOne: The simplest source and sink: two arrows move one proton.
An empty orbital is a sink: one arrow, nothing breaks.
Anion to cation: the arrow runs from minus to plus.
A neutral source, then a proton transfer to finish.

problemSets.title: Formal charge and octets
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Make a bond to a full atom and another bond must break.
problemSets.conceptCard:
Hydrogen holds **two** electrons; C, N, O and F hold **eight**. If an arrow gives an atom a new bond and it is already full, a second arrow must take a bond away.

**Formal charge** = valence electrons − lone-pair electrons − bonds.

- O with **three bonds** and one lone pair: **+**
- N with **four bonds**: **+**
- C with **three bonds** and no lone pair: **+**

setItems.whyThisOne: Where does each charge come from? Count oxygen and chlorine.
The positive charge moves from oxygen to nitrogen.
A bond breaks first: carbon never has five bonds.

problemSets.title: Resonance
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Resonance arrows move π bonds and lone pairs; atoms never move.
problemSets.conceptCard:
Resonance forms are two drawings of **one** species. Between them, only **lone pairs** and **π bonds** move: no σ bond breaks, no atom moves.

- A lone pair next to a π bond pushes in; the π bond moves out.
- A π bond next to a positive carbon slides over.

The real species is a blend. Forms with the negative charge on the **more electronegative** atom, and with full octets, count most.

setItems.whyThisOne: Two identical forms: the charge is shared.
Carbon or oxygen? Oxygen takes most of the charge.
One arrow; the positive charge itself never moves along it.
A neutral molecule with an important charge-separated form.
Nitrogen cannot have five bonds, so the charge must be shared.

problemSets.title: Proton transfer and pKa
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Protons move from the stronger acid to the stronger base.
problemSets.conceptCard:
Every proton transfer is **two arrows**: base lone pair → H, then H–A bond → A.

The equilibrium lies on the side of the **weaker acid** (higher pKa). Useful values:

- H₃O⁺ −1.7, acetic acid 4.8, ammonium 9.2, phenol 10
- water 15.7, ethanol 16

A conjugate base whose charge is **shared by resonance** is weaker, so its acid is stronger.

setItems.whyThisOne: Eleven pKa units downhill: acetate's charge is shared.
The ring shares the charge: phenol is acidic.
Acid activates a carbonyl: draw the carbocation form.
Which way does it go? Find the base first.

problemSets.title: Checkpoint
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Sources, sinks, octets, resonance and proton transfer, mixed.
problemSets.conceptCard: Reactions from every set, shuffled, names hidden until you finish. Three attempts per step.

setItems.whyThisOne: A nucleophile, then a proton transfer.
Which way does the bond break?
Only π bonds and lone pairs move.
Base to proton, bond to oxygen.
Protonate, then the resonance form.
